prediction_scored: uninformative. The design's standard error (about 0.44 points per 5 minutes) gave about 10% power against the predicted upper slope of +0.3, so the registration could not have produced support. The point estimate is not stable: weighting by CHS precision gives +0.19, dropping Manhattan gives +0.67.
settle: Individual-level data linking commute time to depression (a survey with both items), or a panel around a change in commute time; neighbourhood-level aggregates in NYC lack the power for the effect size the research reports. (A PUMS linkage cannot supply depression and was dropped.)

notes: Across 42 UHF neighbourhoods mean one-way commute time (ACS 2015-19) ranges from 25.7 minutes (Greenwich Village-SoHo) to 50.2 minutes (Rockaways). Adjusted for poverty and subway access, depression changes by -0.77 (-1.63 to +0.10) points per 5 minutes; unadjusted -0.45 (-1.23 to +0.32); poverty only -0.76 (-1.38 to -0.14); with borough fixed effects -0.55 (-1.73 to +0.62). The share commuting 60 minutes or more gives -0.64 (-1.72 to +0.43) points per 10 points of share. Manhattan neighbourhoods have short commutes and above-predicted depression, which pulls the slope down. Secondary outcomes (registered as reported only): no exercise in the past 30 days rises +2.20 (+1.19 to +3.22) points per 5 minutes and obesity +4.04 (+2.79 to +5.28) points per 5 minutes, both adjusted. These are far larger than any commute effect the research implies, and they repeat the pattern of mob-active-commute-obesity: long-commute neighbourhoods are outer, car- and bus-dependent and differ in composition. They are associations, not tests. The ACS commute data were read from the Census summary files because the Census API now requires a key; the ZCTA crosswalk matched 214 ZCTAs.
